The Home Depot · Price Adjustments

A routine discount had become a workaround.

To apply a routine discount, associates printed a receipt, aborted the order, and rebuilt it in another app. I designed a markdown workflow in Order Up around how associates actually worked: switching tasks, returning to an order, and explaining the price to a customer.

Role
Staff UX Designer
Scope
Discovery across 12 stores, markdown interactions, and usability testing
Key decision
A fly-out preserves cart context while an associate applies a markdown
Outcome
A 50-store pilot followed by chain-wide rollout; reported impact remains directional

I — Inspiration

An everyday discount meant starting checkout again

A competitor price match or damaged-item discount was a routine customer request. Order Up did not give associates a consistent way to handle it, and the official reason codes did not cover the situations they encountered.

Most often, associates printed a receipt, aborted the order, opened another order-management app, and scanned the receipt to repopulate the order. Only then could they apply the price adjustment and finish checkout.

Observation and interviews across 12 stores revealed both the workaround and the judgment behind it. Managers trusted associates to make good calls; the product needed to make those calls easier to carry out.

D — Design Process

Testing favored a fly-out that kept the order visible

The key decision was the form factor. I prototyped modals, fly-outs, inline inputs, and separate pages, then took the options to stores to test with associates.

An associate might leave the order screen to use another app or take a phone call, then return to finish the transaction. They needed to recognize the item and recover their place quickly. Modals and some fly-outs covered the item being adjusted, making that harder.

Testing favored an anchored fly-out that kept the relevant item visible. I refined the layout around that finding and used “markdown,” the term associates already knew, rather than “adjustment.”

E — Engagement

Keep associate judgment and business controls together

Operations partners supplied the rules the interaction had to preserve: manager approval above $50, a store satisfaction budget, and allocation across SKUs for an order-level markdown. Those constraints were part of the experience, not details to append after the interface was chosen.

I worked within those rules while preserving the flexibility managers expected associates to have. The design needed to handle both item-level and order-level markdowns, show the resulting calculation, and make approval requirements clear.

A — Action

Keep the calculation beside the conversation

I developed apply, update, and remove paths for item-level and order-level markdowns. The cart retained the original price, discount, and updated total so associates could review the change and explain it to the customer.

S — Success

From a 50-store pilot to chain-wide rollout

The markdown feature was piloted in 50 stores, then rolled out to all Home Depot stores. At 30, 60, and 90 days after launch, reported outcomes included lower transaction times, reduced shrink, stronger standard-procedure adoption, and associates feeling more empowered.

Reported outcomes were directional; exact figures are unavailable.

My takeaway: preserving order context and using the associate’s terminology made the approval rules easier to work within. Flexibility and business controls belonged in the same workflow.
